common_name: Pink Dragon Alocasia (Salmon-Stemmed Dragon Scale Alocasia)

planting.note: Divide rhizome offsets or plant container-grown starts in bright indirect light in a chunky, fast-draining aroid mix; keep evenly moist but never waterlogged, since this cultivar shares the baginda lineage's sensitivity to root rot in soggy soil.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light in a fast-draining aroid mix, protecting the foliage from direct midday sun. Pink Dragon is distinguished from other jewel alocasias in the collection by its tall, pale salmon-pink petioles that rise dramatically beneath thick, glossy, dark green leaves boldly veined in contrasting silvery white. Leaf undersides show a purplish-green cast, and the overall silhouette is more upright and taller than the shorter, ground-hugging Dragon Scale and Silver Dragon forms of Alocasia baginda from which it was selected. Provide high humidity and steady warmth above 60F, and reduce watering through winter dormancy.
sources: Royal Horticultural Society — Alocasia 'Pink Dragon' plant profile

common_name: Yucatan Princess Elephant Ear (Puckered Gray-Green Alocasia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown starts after frost danger has passed in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in part shade with some morning sun; this large-growing cultivar rewards steady moisture and monthly feeding during the warm season with rapid, towering growth.

directions: Plant in part shade with well-drained but consistently moist soil; Yucatan Princess is one of the largest landscape alocasias available, capable of reaching 8 feet tall with a 5-foot spread on strong, sturdy stems. The heavily puckered, patent-leather-glossy leaves are gray-green above with striking maroon-to-chocolate-brown undersides and petioles, a color combination not found on the dataset's other large upright elephant ears. Its scale and bold quilted texture make it a signature specimen plant for Gulf Coast tropical borders and large containers, though potted specimens stay considerably shorter than in-ground plants.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox — Alocasia sarawakensis 'Yucatan Princess'
Scott Arboretum of Swarthmore College — Plant of the Week, Alocasia sarawakensis 'Yucatan Princess'

planting.note: Divide basal offsets or plant small container starts in bright indirect light in a well-drained, chunky aroid mix; this vigorously clumping dwarf cultivar fills a pot quickly and is easy to propagate compared to slower-growing jewel alocasias.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light with consistent moisture and high humidity; Tiny Dancer is a true dwarf, staying under 18 inches tall with small, glossy, distinctly teardrop-shaped emerald-green leaves carried on thin, wiry, arching petioles, a markedly finer-textured and more diminutive habit than the standard African Mask type Polly or the larger jewel alocasias already in the collection. It branches freely at the base, quickly forming a dense, multi-stemmed clump ideal for small pots, terrariums, and tabletop display. Bred by aroid hybridizer LariAnn Garner, it is often mislabeled in the trade as Alocasia reginula or Alocasia cuprea.
sources: International Aroid Society — LariAnn Garner Alocasia hybrid introductions

planting.note: Divide offsets or plant container-grown starts after frost danger has passed in rich, evenly moist soil in partial sun to light shade; brighter light intensifies the yellow petiole and vein color on this selection more than on green-stemmed giant taro.

directions: Plant in partial sun to light shade with rich, consistently moist soil; this selection of giant taro is set apart from the plain green species and from 'Variegata' and 'Borneo Giant' by its bright, glowing yellow leaf stalks and leaf veins, which contrast sharply against the broad, otherwise green, upward-pointing leaf blades. The yellow coloring intensifies with more direct sun exposure than the species typically tolerates, making it a strong architectural accent for bright tropical borders and poolside plantings. Growth habit and enormous mature leaf size otherwise match the species, and it shares the same cold response, dying back to a mulched, surviving root mass below zone 9.
sources: National Parks Board Singapore, FloraFaunaWeb — Alocasia macrorrhizos 'Lutea'

common_name: Coal Miner Elephant Ear (Velvet-Patina Black Colocasia)

planting.note: Divide tubers or plant container-grown starts in spring in consistently moist, fertile soil in partial shade, which deepens the near-black leaf coloring; this selection also emerges earlier in spring and proved hardier in cold-climate trials than several other dark-leaved colocasias.

directions: Grow in partial shade with steady moisture and rich soil; Coal Miner produces large, deep olive-black leaves with a distinctive velvety, satin-patina sheen on newly emerging foliage, setting it apart from the more matte, medium-green-based black pattern of Illustris already in the collection and from the glossier near-black of Black Magic and Diamond Head. It grows notably taller and emerges roughly two months earlier in spring than Illustris, and clumps more slowly without Illustris's aggressive underground spread. A 2007 Plant Delights/Juniper Level Botanic Garden introduction, it also ranks among the more cold-hardy dark colocasias in field trials.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery — Colocasia esculenta 'Coal Miner' introduction notes
